'''Sau Lan Wu''' ([[Chinese language|Chinese]]: 吳秀蘭; born May 11, 1940) is a Chinese-American [[particle physics|particle physicist]] and the Enrico Fermi Distinguished Professor of Physics at the [[University of Wisconsin-Madison]]. She made important contributions towards the discovery of the [[J/psi particle]], which provided experimental evidence for the existence of the [[charm quark]], and the [[gluon]], the vector boson of the [[strong force]] in the [[Standard Model]] of physics.<ref>{{cite book |author1=S. Braibant |author2=G. Giacomelli |author3=M. Spurio |year=2009 |title=Particles and Fundamental Interactions: An Introduction to Particle Physics |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0Pp-f0G9_9sC&pg=PA314 |pages=313–314 |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] |isbn=978-94-007-2463-1}}</ref> Her team located at the European Organization for Nuclear Research ([[CERN]]), using data collected at the [[Large Hadron Collider]] (LHC), was part of the international effort in the discovery of a boson consistent with the [[Higgs boson]].<ref name="higg">{{cite web|url=http://www.atlas.ch/news/2012/atlas-and-the-higgs.html|title=ATLAS and the Higgs|publisher=CERN|date=October 2012|access-date=6 March 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130215192435/http://www.atlas.ch/news/2012/atlas-and-the-higgs.html|archive-date=15 February 2013}}</ref>

==Early life==
Wu was born in the early 1940s during the Japanese occupation of [[Hong Kong]] and went to [[Vassar College]] in 1960 with a full scholarship for her undergraduate degree.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/sau-lan-wus-three-major-physics-discoveries-and-counting-20180718/|title=Sau Lan Wu's Three Major Physics Discoveries and Counting|website=Quanta Magazine|language=en|access-date=2020-03-07}}</ref> Initially, she dreamed of becoming a painter, but was inspired by [[Marie Curie]] to devote her life to physics. During her years at Vassar, she spent a summer at [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]] where the science of [[particle physics]] captivated her.<ref name=vassar1>{{cite web|url= http://vq.vassar.edu/issues/2003/03/beyond-vassar/charmed-life.html|title=A Charmed Life|author=Dawson, Lindsay|publisher=Vassar Alumnae Quarterly|date=Summer 2003|access-date=16 January 2013}}</ref>

During her freshman year she and a few more of her Vassar schoolmates were invited to the [[White House]] for an [[Easter]] function and met [[Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis|Jacqueline Kennedy]], a Vassar alumna (class of 1951). She first experienced racial discrimination when visiting the [[Supreme Court of the United States|Supreme Court]] and was confronted with the choice of "black" or "white" on the door to the restroom.

==Academic background==
Wu graduated from Vassar College (1963) with an [[Bachelor of Arts|A.B.]] in physics.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://vq.vassar.edu/issues/2013/01/beyond-vassar/joy-of-discovery.html|title=The Joy of Discovery: Sau Lan Wu '63 - Vassar, the Alumnae/i Quarterly|website=vq.vassar.edu|access-date=2020-03-07}}</ref> In 1964, Wu received her M.A. in physics as part of the first cohort of women awarded graduate degrees directly by [[Harvard University]]. After earning a [[Ph.D.]] (1970) in physics from [[Harvard University]], she conducted research at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]], [[DESY]] and the [[University of Wisconsin-Madison]], where she was the Enrico Fermi Distinguished Professor of Physics until her retirement in 2026.<ref name=":1" /> Since 1986, Wu has been the Visiting Scientist at CERN conducting research with the LHC as part of the [[ATLAS experiment|ATLAS]] team.<ref name=CWP>{{cite web|url= http://cwp.library.ucla.edu/Phase2/Wu,_Sau_Lan@892345678.html|title=Sau Lan Wu|author=Contributions of 20th Century Women to Physics at UCLA|date=16 March 2001|access-date=16 January 2013}}</ref>

==Achievements==

===J/psi===
Sau Lan was part of the team led by [[Samuel C.C. Ting]] at MIT who discovered the [[J/psi]] particle in 1974,<ref name=CWP/> for which Ting was awarded the 1976 [[Nobel Prize]] in Physics together with [[Burton Richter]].<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/1976/|title=The Nobel Prize in Physics 1976|publisher=Nobel Prize|access-date=6 March 2013}}</ref> The MIT team where Sau Lan Wu was a postdoc at the time took advantage of the [[Alternating Gradient Synchrotron]] accelerator at [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]] with high-intensity proton beams, which bombarded a stationary target to produce showers of particles that were detected by particle detectors. They discovered a strong peak in electron-positron [[Invariant mass]] at an energy of 3.1 billion electron volts ([[GeV]]). This led them to suspect that they had discovered a new stable particle decaying into electron-positron pairs, the same one found by Richter at the [[SPEAR]] collider in the [[SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory]].

===Gluon===

Wu was a key contributor to the discovery of the [[gluon]]<ref>{{cite web |last=Riesselmann |first=Kurt |title=Gluon discovery |url=https://www.symmetrymagazine.org/article/august-2005/gluon-discovery |website=[[Symmetry (magazine)|Symmetry]] |date=2005-08-01 |access-date=2026-07-28 }}</ref>, a particle that binds, or glues, quarks together to form protons and neutrons.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Ellis|first=John|title=Those were the days: discovering the gluon|journal=CERN Courier|date=July 2009|volume=49|issue=6|pages=15–17|url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/1734399}}</ref> For her effort, Sau Lan Wu and her collaborators were awarded the 1995 [[European Physical Society]] [[High Energy and Particle Physics Prize]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://eps-hepp.web.cern.ch/eps-hepp/hepp-prize-awards.php|title=The High Energy and Particle Physics Prizes|publisher=European Physical Society|access-date=6 March 2013|archive-date=26 May 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080526132255/http://eps-hepp.web.cern.ch/eps-hepp/hepp-prize-awards.php}}</ref> The smoking gun signature proving the existence of the gluon were the so-called 'three [[Jet (particle physics)|jet]] events' occurring in electron-positron annihilation into a quark-antiquark pair, where an additional gluon is radiated from one of the quarks, creating the third jet. In the late 1970s Wu joined the [[TASSO collaboration|TASSO Collaboration]] that operated at the [[PETRA]] accelerator at [[DESY]].  In 1979 she published a paper with George Zobernig on a method of three-jet analysis in electron-positron annihilation,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wu|first1=Sau Lan|last2=Zobernig|first2=Georg|date=1979|title=A method of three-jet analysis in electron-positron annihilation|url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF01474124|journal=Z. Phys. C|language=en|volume=2|issue=2|pages=107–110|doi=10.1007/BF01474124|s2cid=121082519 |issn=0170-9739|url-access=subscription}}</ref> that was used in the following publication with the entire TASSO Collaboration,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=TASSO Collaboration|date=1979|title=Tests for planar events in electron-positron annihilation|journal=Physics Letters B|volume=82|issue=1|pages=134–138|doi=10.1016/0370-2693(79)90444-1|issn=0370-2693}}</ref> regarded as the first evidence of a gluon.

[[File:EPS prize 1995 Gluon.png|thumb|Award certificate of 1995 EPS Physics Prize in Brussels, Belgium.]]
[[File:EPS 1995 recipients.png|thumb|The four Prize Recipients at the ceremony of the 1995 European Physical Society High Energy and Particle Physics Prize in Brussels, Belgium. Front row: Günter Wolf and Sau Lan Wu; second row: Björn Wiik and Paul Söding.]]

Working from first principles, Wu calculated that a collision energy of roughly 22 [[Electronvolt|GeV]] would be needed to cleanly resolve a three-jet signature, close to PETRA's planned operating energy, and worked out with her postdoctoral researcher Georg Zobernig how to disentangle the three overlapping jets, based on the insight that the quark, antiquark, and gluon jets must lie in a common "event plane."<ref name="soding1995">{{cite conference|last1=Söding|first1=Paul|last2=Wiik|first2=Bjørn|last3=Wolf|first3=Günter|last4=Wu|first4=Sau Lan|title=The First Evidence for Three-Jet Events in e+e- Collisions at PETRA – First Direct Observation of the Gluon|book-title=Proceedings of the International Europhysics Conference on High Energy Physics|date=2 August 1995|location=Brussels, Belgium|pages=3–10|url=https://lib-extopc.kek.jp/preprints/PDF/1996/9610/9610251.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Wu|first=Sau Lan|title=e+e– Physics at PETRA – The First Five Years|journal=Physics Reports|date=1984|volume=107|issue=2|pages=59–324|doi=10.1016/0370-1573(84)90104-9}}</ref>

When the PETRA accelerator's energy first exceeded Wu's calculated threshold in May–June 1979, Wu and Zobernig used their method to identify the first three-jet event recorded at PETRA.<ref name="soding1995"/> [[Bjørn Wiik]] presented the result, crediting Wu and Zobernig, at the "Neutrino '79" conference in Bergen, Norway, in June 1979, where TASSO's three-jet observation was the only such result among the four PETRA experiments; Wu and Zobernig documented the finding that month in TASSO Note No. 84, and further three-jet events were presented by [[Paul Söding]] at the European Physical Society Conference in Geneva the following month.<ref name="soding1995"/> The other three PETRA collaborations—JADE, Mark J, and [[PLUTO experiment|PLUTO]]—developed comparable analyses over the following months, and all four experiments reported confirming evidence by the International Symposium on Lepton-Photon Interactions at [[Fermilab]] in August 1979.<ref name="soding1995"/> In September 1980, using the same three-jet analysis techniques, TASSO further established that the new particle carried [[Spin (physics)|spin]] 1, as predicted for the gluon, completing its experimental identification.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Wu|first=Sau Lan|title=The Discovery of Gluons|journal=AIP Conference Proceedings|date=1994|volume=300|pages=598–623|doi=10.1063/1.45418}}</ref>

The 1995 European Physical Society High Energy and Particle Physics Prize was awarded to [[Paul Söding]], [[Bjørn Wiik]], Günter Wolf, and Sau Lan Wu of the TASSO Collaboration for this work, and Wu delivered the acceptance speech on behalf of the recipients; the Society separately recognized all four PETRA experiments for their collective experimental confirmation of the gluon.<ref name="soding1995"/><ref>{{cite journal|title=1995 EPS High Energy & Particle Physics Prize|journal=Europhysics News|date=1995|volume=26|issue=4|page=95|url=https://www.europhysicsnews.org/articles/epn/pdf/1995/04/epn19952604p95.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Gluon Discovery Honoured|journal=Europhysics News|date=1995|volume=26|issue=4|page=88|url=https://www.europhysicsnews.org/articles/epn/pdf/1995/04/epn19952604p88.pdf}}</ref>

===Higgs boson===
Wu's team in Wisconsin was the first American group to join the [[ATLAS Collaboration]] at [[CERN]], in 1993,<ref name=":2">{{Cite news|last=Overbye|first=Dennis|date=2013-03-05|title=Chasing the Higgs|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/03/05/science/chasing-the-higgs-boson-how-2-teams-of-rivals-at-CERN-searched-for-physics-most-elusive-particle.html|access-date=2021-08-25|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> however, her hunt for the Higgs Boson had started earlier at the [[Large Electron–Positron Collider|Large Electron–Positron (LEP) Collider]] also at [[CERN]]. Together with other scientists at LEP they observed a number of Higgs boson candidates, but the observation was not statistically significant and they were only able to set a lower limit on the mass of the hypothetical Higgs Boson particle at 114.4 GeV (at the 95% confidence level).<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2003-07-17|title=Search for the Standard Model Higgs boson at LEP|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0370269303006142|journal=Physics Letters B|language=en|volume=565|pages=61–75|doi=10.1016/S0370-2693(03)00614-2 |arxiv=hep-ex/0306033 |issn=0370-2693|hdl=11567/390137|hdl-access=free|last1=Abbiendi |first1=G. |s2cid=118929428 }}</ref> In 2000 CERN had shut the LEP collider so that the [[Large Hadron Collider]] could be built in its place.


On July 4, 2012, following the immense efforts of the [[ATLAS Collaboration|ATLAS]] and [[Compact Muon Solenoid|CMS]] Collaborations, CERN announced the [[Higgs boson|discovery of a boson]] consistent with the predicted characters of Higgs boson with a mass of 125 GeV. This was a statistically significant discovery at the level of 5-sigma, a term meaning that the odds it occurred by chance are less than 1 in 3.5 million.<ref name="higg" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.symmetrymagazine.org/article/when-was-the-higgs-actually-discovered|title=When was the Higgs actually discovered?|last=Charley|first=Sarah|website=symmetry magazine|date=3 July 2017 |language=en|access-date=2020-03-07}}</ref> This discovery completes the [[Standard Model]] of particle physics which explains most of the phenomena in the visible [[Universe]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://public.web.cern.ch/public/|title=A question of spin for the new boson|publisher=CERN|date=6 March 2013|access-date=6 March 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121206235458/http://public.web.cern.ch/public/|archive-date=6 December 2012}}</ref> 

Wu is credited as a significant contributor to the discovery with her Wisconsin's group work on the two key decay channels that led to the discovery of the Higgs boson, the decay of the Higgs boson into two gamma-rays (H→ɣɣ), and the decay of the Higgs boson into four [[lepton]]s (H→ZZ*→4ℓ).<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://massivesci.com/articles/meet-the-physicist-who-helped-discover-three-fundamental-particles/|title=Meet Sau Lan Wu, the physicist who helped discover three fundamental particles|last=|first=|date=5 April 2017|website=Massive Science|access-date=2020-03-07}}</ref>

In March 2013, Wu was pictured with [[Peter Higgs]] and a few other leading CERN researchers on the front page of the ''Science Times'' section of ''[[The New York Times]]'' for Dennis Overbye's feature "Chasing the Higgs".<ref>{{Cite news|last=Overbye|first=Dennis|author-link=Dennis Overbye|title=Chasing the Higgs Boson: How 2 Teams of Rivals Searched for Physics' Most Elusive Particle |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/03/05/science/chasing-the-higgs-boson-how-2-teams-of-rivals-at-cern-searched-for-physics-most-elusive-particle.html|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=2013-03-05|access-date=2026-07-28}}</ref>

In her later research, Wu worked on applications of [[artificial intelligence]] and [[quantum computing]] in high-energy physics. She was corresponding author of a 2021 study applying a quantum-kernel machine-learning method to Higgs-boson production in association with top quarks at the LHC.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wu|first1=Sau Lan|last2=Sun|first2=Shaojun|last3=Guan|first3=Wen|last4=Zhou|first4=Chen|last5=Chan|first5=Jay|last6=Cheng|first6=Chi Lung|last7=Pham|first7=Tuan|last8=Qian|first8=Yan|last9=Wang|first9=Alex Zeng|last10=Zhang|first10=Rui|last11=Livny|first11=Miron|display-authors=3|date=2021|title=Application of quantum machine learning using the quantum kernel algorithm on high energy physics analysis at the LHC|journal=Physical Review Research|volume=3|issue=3|article-number=033221|doi=10.1103/PhysRevResearch.3.033221|arxiv=2104.05059|bibcode=2021PhRvR...3c3221W}}</ref> In 2022, at the invitation of ''[[Nature Reviews Physics]]'', Wu and Shinjae Yoo published an article on the challenges and opportunities of [[quantum machine learning]] in high-energy physics.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wu|first1=Sau Lan|last2=Yoo|first2=Shinjae|date=2022|title=Challenges and opportunities in quantum machine learning for high-energy physics|journal=Nature Reviews Physics|volume=4|issue=3|pages=143–144|doi=10.1038/s42254-022-00425-7|bibcode=2022NatRP...4..143W}}</ref>

=== Mentorship ===
Sau Lan Wu has supervised 65 doctoral students and mentored numerous postdoctoral researchers across the TASSO, ALEPH, BaBar, and ATLAS experiments. .<ref name=":0" /> As of 2026, 42 of her former students and postdoctoral researchers had become university faculty members, 18 had obtained permanent staff positions at major high-energy-physics laboratories, and 34 held positions in industry.

==Honors==
*Outstanding Junior Investigator Award of U.S. Department of Energy, 1980
*Romnes Faculty Award, University of Wisconsin, Madison 1981
*Hilldale Professorship, University of Wisconsin, Madison 1991
*Fellow, [[American Physical Society]] 1992
*[[High Energy and Particle Physics Prize]] of the [[European Physical Society]] 1995, with [[Paul Söding]], [[Björn Wiik]], and Günter Wolf, for the discovery of the gluon.
*Fellow, American Academy of Arts and Sciences 1996
*Vilas Professorship, University of Wisconsin, Madison 1998<ref name=CWP/>
*Wu delivered Vassar College's 150th Commencement Address in 2014, becoming the first physicist to give the college's commencement address. 
*Sau Lan Wu has been featured in several books as an inspiring scientist figure for young students. The books include : A ''New York Times'' Best Seller "Women in Science – 50 fearless pioneers who changed the world",<ref>{{cite book | last=Ignotofsky | first=Rachel | title=Women in Science | publisher=Ten Speed Press | publication-place=Berkeley, CA | date=July 2016 |url=https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/534776/women-in-science-by-rachel-ignotofsky/ | isbn=978-1-60774-976-9}}</ref> "This Little Scientist : A Discovery Primer",<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/This-Little-Scientist/Joan-Holub/This-Little/9781534401082 |title=This Little Scientist |date=2018-09-25 |isbn=978-1-5344-0108-2 |language=en|last1=Holub |first1=Joan |publisher=Little Simon }}</ref> "Good Night Stories for Rebel Girls: 100 Immigrant Women Who Changed the World",<ref>{{Cite web |title=Good Night Stories for Rebel Girls: 100 Immigrant Women Who Changed the World {{!}} Rebel Girls |url=https://www.rebelgirls.com/products/good-night-stories-for-rebel-girls-100-immigrant-women-who-changed-the-world |access-date=2022-06-10 |website=www.rebelgirls.com |language=en-US}}</ref> "How to Be Extraordinary",<ref>{{cite book | last=Sirdeshpande | first=Rashmi | author-link=Rashmi Sirdeshpande | others=Illustrated by Annabel Tempest | title=How to Be Extraordinary | publisher=Puffin | date=August 2019 | isbn=978-0-241-38540-1 }}</ref> "Scientists Alphabet Book by Christi Sperber", "Bold Women in Science: 15 Women in History You Should Know" by Danni Washington and "50 Women in Technology" by Georgina Ferry, Bridget Greenwood and Ines Almeida.
*Minor planet 177770 SaulanWu, discovered by astronomers with the Mount Lemmon Survey in 2005, was named in her honor.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Small-Body Database Lookup |url=https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/tools/sbdb_lookup.html#/?sstr=SaulanWu |access-date=2022-06-10 |website=ssd.jpl.nasa.gov}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-06-10 |title=Sau Lan Wu honored with named planet |url=https://www.physics.wisc.edu/2022/06/10/sau-lan-wu-honored-with-named-planet/ |access-date=2022-06-11 |website=Department of Physics |language=en-US}}</ref> The official naming citation was published by International Astronomical Union's WG Small Body Nomenclature (WGSBN) bulletin and [[Minor Planet Center]] on 23 May 2022.<ref>{{Cite web |title=IAU Minor Planet Center |url=https://minorplanetcenter.net/db_search/show_object?object_id=177770 |access-date=2022-06-10 |website=minorplanetcenter.net}}</ref>
*[[Phi Beta Kappa]] Excellence in Teaching Award, University of Wisconsin–Madison, 2021.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-04-20 |title=Phi Beta Kappa inducts 229 at ceremony |url=https://news.wisc.edu/phi-beta-kappa-inducts-229-at-ceremony/ |access-date=2026-07-26 |website=University of Wisconsin–Madison News}}</ref>
*Distinguished Achievement Award, Alumnae/i Association of Vassar College, 2023.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-06-13 |title=AAVC Announces 2023 Honorees |url=https://www.vassar.edu/news/aavc-announces-2023-honorees |access-date=2026-07-26 |website=Vassar College}}</ref>
*[[Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics]], 2025, as a member of the [[ATLAS experiment|ATLAS Collaboration]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=ATLAS Collaboration |url=https://breakthroughprize.org/Laureates/1/L3993 |access-date=2026-07-26 |website=Breakthrough Prize}}</ref>
